abstract: The paper gives a review of the present state of knowledge and opinion in the field of partial discharges In power transformers. After indicating how such discharges arise, the different methods of measurement are considered and the various techniques and necessary precautions are reviewed. The interpretation of the measurements and test results Is then dealt with and this leads on to the difficult problem of locating the source of a discharge. The methods at present available are reviewed and their relative advantages and disadvantages considered. Finally the question of voltage test levels and durations Is reviewed and the conclusion reached that any proposal for a test specification based on discharge measurements is quite premature, although such measurements can be of great value to the designer.

abstract: Not too much stress should be laid on manufacturing for local conditions only for ultimately it is of great importance to South Africa to be able to export its products. Consequently manufacturers should have the greatest regard for manufacturing specifically to international standards. The South African National Committee on the other hand was doing its utmost to see that IEC specifications incorporated the requirements to meet local operating conditions. Most of the anomalies which occur with testing say insulation in this country were due to the fact that standard test conditions were not adhered to. On the other hand this was still work to be done to determine the appropriate correction factors for local conditions of testing to cover variations of temperature, pressure and humidity.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Present day techniques for the design and construction of electrical apparatus for use in explosive atmospheres are discussed. Distinction is made between apparatuses for use in localities where gases and vapours, flammable dusts, or flammable fibres can occur in the air, and also between apparatuses for localities where an explosion hazard can occur under normal conditions or under abnormal conditions only. Static electricity is discussed, as well as problems of installation and maintenance of equipment.

abstract: A.W. Richards: To date very little work has been done on the problem of electrical equipment operating in areas where flammable or explosive substances that burn without an external oxygen source are present. The stability range of such materials is extremely wide and because of this it is difficult to prescribe equipment suitable for general use. Ideally, electrical equipment to be used in such areas should be tailored to suit the environment. In certain cases intrinsically safe equipment may be suitable but it must be borne in mind that the ignition energies of many explosive substances are well below those that may be released in most intrinsically safe circuits.

abstract: Diamond, as the hardest material known to man, is playing an increasingly important role in modern industry. It has proved itself the most efficient material for the shaping and fashioning, to an extremely high degree of accuracy, a wide range of materials normally extremely difficult to machine. The electrical industry is no exception to this general advance of diamond technology. One of the most important uses of diamond is in the wire drawing Industry where only diamond is able to produce the finer gauges of wire. From electric light bulb filaments to 5 micron diameter wire for computer applications, diamond is used as the vehicle for drawing the wire. The growth of the semi-conductor and transistor industries has greatly accelerated the use of industrial diamond as a tool for the forming of electrical components. Diamond in its own right can exhibit interesting electrical properties and, In certain circumstances, functions as a semi-conductor.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Failure of insulation, after equipment has been in servce for some time, at values of electric stress well below its accepted breakdown value, is caused by the basic processes of intrinsic and thermal breakdown. Conditions necessary to precipitate these mechanisms are realised by a slow process of erosion caused by internal discharges within the mass of the insulation. This paper discusses briefly the discharge process and the resulting breakdown and indicates directions in which research in this field is progressing at the University of the Witwatersrand.

abstract: Different meanings may be attached to the term high structure depending on the reference level from which the height is measured. To make this statement more explicit let us consider three specific examples of high structures for which lightning data are available. The first of these is the Empire State Building, New York, which has a height of 380 metres (1250 ft) above ground level, the ground being approximately at sea level. The building is not isolated but is surrounded by other tall buildings, so that in effect there is a grouped complex of high structures with the top of the Empire State Building forming its peak.

articleTitle: Power transmission and the constraints of society
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Electricity supply systems in most countries are dependent on high voltage power transmission for purposes of interconnection, bulk power transmission, or economic development of supplies. The main technical features in design are dictated by such factors as distance, amount of energy to be transmitted, and emergency demands. However, the design may also be considerably affected by conditions determined by the society dependent on the supply system, who may express views and impose restrictions in such aspects as costs, appearance, noise emission, and the various types of electrical interference. The lecture will consider the impact of these requirements of the community on the design, operation and economics of power transmission systems.

abstract: The problems associated with high-voltage testing and research, would in most cases be viewed by manufacturers in South Africa, from the standpoints of scope and cost, and of equipment and manpower requirements. In turn these are related to following the needs of existing specifications with regard to routine and type testing of high-voltage equipment. Specifications must of necessity be related to South African conditions and attention is drawn to the need for continual investigation in this respect. As there is always a desire to improve upon methods of testing, research is done on this, and the outcome is various suggested tests, not currently the subject of specifications. Some of these, chiefly concerned with discharge testing, are discussed. Comment is made on existing testing facilities of manufacturers in South Africa. Finally the difficulties in determining requirements of the future are considered.

articleTitle: Paper 7 the measurement of lightning ground flash density
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The thunderstorm day as a unit of measurement of lightning activity is known to be inadequate, especially for purposes of comparison of the operation of transmission systems in lightning areas; consequently means of measuring the lightning ground flash density directly are being urgently sought and developed. This paper describes a few forms of lightning flash counter, some of which are being considered for international use, and then proceeds to state and derive the theory upon which their successful application depends. The variations of the electrostatic field intensity with time In respect of the leader and return portions of a stroke of lightning are postulated, and the response of RC measuring circuits is discussed, especially in regard to the determination of the effective range. It is concluded that the measurement of the lightning ground flash density can be accomplished by means of lightning flash counters, but the design characteristics have to be carefully considered. The effective range can be determined only by a statistical analysis of observations and further work on this aspect Is proceeding.

articleTitle: Paper I high-voltage testing in the promotion of standardization
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The new laboratory of the South African Bureau of Standards is to accommodate a 3.2-MV, 160-kJ impulse generator, a 360-kV cascaded transformer set, and a transformer (with an output voltage variable from 250 V to 33 300 V in 1.4 per cent steps and capable of delivering a follow current of 500 A with a regulation not exceeding 10 per cent for the most frequently used range of test voltages) for the testing of lightning arresters. The testing of lightning arresters Is dealt with, with special reference to the mathematical principle of obtaining a 8/20 μs surge current wave. Calculation of parameters for a simulated discharge of 150 miles of transmission line is given for a 132-kV system, and a comparison is made between a transmission line discharge test and a conventional long duration test with a rectangular wave of 2000 μs duration and 150 A, 300 A, or 500 A current amplitude. Impulse testing of transformers is critically reviewed in the light of the modern tendency to design transformers with high input capacitance, and a circuit Is discussed in which a 1.2/50 μs impulse can be obtained for high-capacitance windings. Finally the testing of insulators at altitudes up to 6000 ft is discussed with special reference to the correction of flashover values to sea level conditions. Wet tests are criticised, and it is suggested that the new climate control room for insulators may aid in the working out of a reliable pollution test to prove insulator performance.

abstract: Dactyloscopy or ‘finger display’ is a classical aid of the criminal police. There is a basic difference between personal dactyloscopy and scene-of-the-crime dactyloscopy. Personal dactyloscopy is used to identify persons by means of all 10 finger-prints. It is made in accordance with the Galton-Henry ten-finger collection classification method. This system, which the Zurich County Police in Switzerland also uses, ensures a collection of a size permitting efficient identification of persons. Scene-of-the-crime dactyloscopy, on the other hand, employs dactyloscopy clues in crime detection. Systematic interpretation of the clues is carried out by comparing them with those in the single finger collection. Only under certain clue-conditions is it occasionally possible to use the ten-finger collection for this purpose.
